papers.core_contribution: The paper extracts mechanistic circuits for extractive QA, revealing differences between context and memory faithfulness circuits, and uses insights from the circuits to develop ATTNATTRIB for data attribution and model steering towards context faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic circuits for extractive QA can be extracted and used for practical applications like data attribution and model steering, enhancing language model performance and faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct circuits are extracted: a context-faithfulness circuit and a memory-faithfulness circuit.
A small set of attention heads in the context circuit perform reliable data attribution by default.
ATTNATTRIB achieves state-of-the-art attribution results on various extractive QA benchmarks.
Using attributions from ATTNATTRIB can steer the model towards context faithfulness, improving performance by up to 9%.
Circuits for context faithfulness are smaller and involve different components compared to memory circuits.
papers.limitation:
The probe dataset is primarily 0-hop, and ATTNATTRIB performs less well on multi-hop QA.
ATTNATTRIB requires white-box access to the model's parameters, so it cannot be applied to blackbox LLMs.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated strategies that combine ATTNATTRIB with retrieval-based attribution.
Designing a probe dataset consisting of multi-hop questions to improve circuit extraction for multi-hop QA.
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to process documents and facilitate question-answering on them. In our paper, we extract mechanistic circuits for this real-world language modeling task: context-augmented language modeling for extractive question-answering (QA) tasks and understand the potential benefits of circuits towards downstream applications such as data attribution to context information. We extract circuits as a function of internal model components (e.g., attention heads, MLPs) using causal mediation analysis techniques. Leveraging the extracted circuits, we first understand the interplay between the model's usage of parametric memory and retrieved context towards a better mechanistic understanding of context-augmented language models. We then identify a small set of attention heads in our circuit which performs reliable data attribution by default, thereby obtaining attribution for free in just the model's forward pass. Using this insight, we then introduce ATTNATTRIB, a fast data attribution algorithm which obtains state-of-the-art attribution results across various extractive QA benchmarks. Finally, we show the possibility to steer the language model towards answering from the context, instead of the parametric memory by using the attribution from ATTNATTRIB as an additional signal during the forward pass. Beyond mechanistic understanding, our paper provides tangible applications of circuits in the form of reliable data attribution and model steering.

papers.title: COMPASS: Context-Modulated PID Attention Steering System for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can contextual hallucinations in LLMs be reduced by dynamically steering attention to retrieved context during generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a lightweight framework that uses a PID controller and a Context Reliance Score to dynamically steer attention to context during generation, reducing hallucinations without retraining or multi-pass decoding.
papers.conclusion: Feedback-driven attention control is a feasible, low-overhead strategy for reducing hallucinations in LLMs, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque interventions.
papers.key_findings:
COMPASS reduces hallucination rates by 2.8–5.8% across benchmarks.
It decreases unsupported span density and improves context overlap metrics.
The method operates efficiently within a single decode stream without requiring model retraining.
Larger models (e.g., LLaMA-2-13B, Mistral-7B) benefit more from attention modulation, likely due to richer redundancy and head-level structure.
The framework provides an interpretable mapping between internal attention signals and model behavior.
papers.limitation:
Head-importance estimation may under-perform in extremely long-context or multi-turn settings where risk accrues gradually without strong local cues.
Gating decisions are made per step without global discourse awareness, so suppression of longer narrative drifts is limited.
Sensitivity to controller hyperparameters (EMA smoothing, hysteresis, PID gains, log-space slew limit and cap) can cause oscillatory activation, unstable convergence, or oversuppression of useful heads.
Computing CRS features and per-layer top-K selection adds modest but non-negligible overhead that can impact latency on smaller GPUs or very long sequences.
future_direction: Integration of richer detector signals that capture semantic coherence.
Formalizing stability guarantees for PID-controlled attention modulation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but factually incorrect statements despite having access to relevant evidence, a failure mode rooted in how they allocate attention between contextual and parametric knowledge. Understanding and steering this internal behavior is key both for trustworthy deployment and for scientific interpretability of model mechanisms. We introduce COMPASS (Context-Modulated PID Attention Steering System), a lightweight, interpretable control framework that embeds a model-based feedback loop directly within decoding. COMPASS quantifies context reliance via a transparent metric, the Context Reliance Score (CRS), which serves as an online probe of how attention heads ground generation in evidence. Using this interpretable signal, a PID controller dynamically modulates attention heads to maintain factual consistency without retraining or multi-pass decoding. Across benchmarks (HotpotQA, XSum, HaluEval, RAGTruth), COMPASS consistently reduces contextual hallucination rates (2.8 to 5.8 percent absolute) while revealing how distinct attention heads contribute to evidence alignment. These results highlight feedback-driven interpretability as a pathway toward scientific understanding of LLM behavior.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Parameters vs. Context: Fine-Grained Control of Knowledge Reliance in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained control over a language model's reliance on its internal parametric knowledge versus external retrieved context in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios, especially when conflicts arise?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CK-PLUG, a plug-and-play inference-time method that uses a novel Confidence Gain metric to detect knowledge conflicts and a single tuning parameter to adjust token probability distributions, enabling fine-grained control over a model's reliance on parametric versus contextual knowledge in RAG.
papers.conclusion: CK-PLUG provides an effective framework for fine-grained control over knowledge reliance in LLMs during RAG, enabling users to balance parametric and contextual knowledge based on scenario needs and improving overall generation reliability.
papers.key_findings:
CK-PLUG enables a wide range of control over knowledge reliance, e.g., adjusting the Memory Recall (MR) ratio from 9.89% to 71.93% on LLAMA3-8B, significantly deviating from the baseline of 42.09%.
In adaptive mode (without manual α setting), CK-PLUG consistently improves performance across six diverse RAG downstream tasks compared to standard RAG baselines.
The method uses a single parameter α for fine-grained control, with MR varying approximately linearly as α changes across different models.
An ablation study shows that the conflict detection module (ConD) is crucial; removing it leads to a noticeable decline in generation quality, especially under extreme modulation settings.
CK-PLUG effectively balances parametric and contextual knowledge, maintaining generation fluency and logical consistency while adjusting knowledge preference.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge. However, conflicts between parametric knowledge and retrieved context pose challenges, particularly when retrieved information is unreliable or the model's internal knowledge is outdated. In such cases, LLMs struggle to determine whether to rely more on their own parameters or the conflicted context. To address this, we propose **CK-PLUG**, a plug-and-play method for controlling LLMs' reliance on parametric and contextual knowledge. We introduce a novel knowledge consistency metric, Confidence Gain, which detects knowledge conflicts by measuring entropy shifts in token probability distributions after context insertion. CK-PLUG then enables fine-grained control over knowledge preference by adjusting the probability distribution of tokens with negative confidence gain through a single tuning parameter. Experiments demonstrate CK-PLUG's ability to significantly regulate knowledge reliance in counterfactual RAG scenarios while maintaining generation fluency and knowledge accuracy. For instance, on Llama3-8B, memory recall (MR) of RAG response can be adjusted within a broad range (9.9%-71.9%), compared to the baseline of 42.1%. Moreover, CK-PLUG supports adaptive control based on the model's confidence in both internal and external knowledge, achieving consistent performance improvements across various general RAG tasks. Our code is available at: $\href{https://github.com/byronBBL/CK-PLUG}{\text{this https URL}}$.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source
papers.research_question: How do LLMs prioritize between their learned parametric knowledge (PK) and external contextual knowledge (CK) when faced with conflicting information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing framework to study how LLMs select between parametric and contextual knowledge, showing that specific activations, especially from mid-layers and relation tokens, correlate with the knowledge source used.
papers.conclusion: Specific model activations correlate with knowledge source selection, and the probing framework generalizes across relation groups, enabling future work on controlling knowledge source behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed, with mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, being crucial for prediction.
The most predictive features for knowledge source selection are those of the relation token in the query.
The knowledge source can be detected directly from the perturbing object token early in the inference process.
MHSA activations are less connected to the used knowledge source than MLP-L2 and MLP-L1 activations.
The probing framework successfully transfers learned knowledge source patterns from one relation group to another, demonstrating generalization.
papers.limitation:
The framework is designed to probe LLMs by introducing contradictions to their learned knowledge and does not account for situations where the knowledge remains unperturbed.
The study primarily measures correlation between activations and knowledge source use, but does not establish an explanation of the underlying process.
The framework uses a conventional subject-relation-object prompt structure, which may introduce biases; exploring alternative prompt structures could yield further insights.
future_direction: Extend the framework to handle cases where both parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge are consistent or not related.
Uncover the underlying mechanisms that govern knowledge source selection in LLMs through experimental designs that manipulate specific model parameters or activations.
Employ a variety of prompt structures to mitigate biases associated with the conventional subject-relation-object format.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often encounter conflicts between their learned, internal (parametric knowledge, PK) and external knowledge provided during inference (contextual knowledge, CK). Understanding how LLMs models prioritize one knowledge source over the other remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel probing framework to explore the mechanisms governing the selection between PK and CK in LLMs. Using controlled prompts designed to contradict the model's PK, we demonstrate that specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed. We evaluate this framework on various LLMs of different sizes and demonstrate that mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, are crucial in predicting knowledge source selection, paving the way for more reliable models capable of handling knowledge conflicts effectively.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs with variations, and reveals that the last token acts as a function vector encoding relation and language, composed in two stages in decoder-only models.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for factual recall, indicating that knowledge evaluation and editing methods need to be adapted for multilingual settings.
papers.key_findings:
The early MLP site for subject enrichment is present in multilingual LLMs, but the late site involves both MLP and attention, unlike English LLMs where only attention dominates.
Subject information flows similarly to monolingual models, but non-subject token flow differs.
In multilingual decoder-only LLMs, both feed-forward and attention sublayers contribute to object extraction, unlike in English autoregressive LLMs where attention modules dominate.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV) encoding both the relation and the output language.
In decoder-only LLMs, the FV is constructed in two distinct phases: first encoding the relation, then incorporating the language.
future_direction: Developing knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition methods tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying how the function vector is altered across languages to understand if models think in English
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Don't Think of the White Bear: Ironic Negation in Transformer Models Under Cognitive Load
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do transformer language models show ironic rebound (increased accessibility of a forbidden concept) versus suppression after a negation instruction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit ironic rebound after negation instructions, with semantic distractors causing the strongest rebound and a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress them, linking cognitive predictions to mechanistic insights.
papers.conclusion: LLMs display ironic rebound after a 'do not mention X' instruction, becoming more likely to output X, with circuit tracing showing sparse middle-layer attention heads amplify the forbidden token under load while early layers suppress it.
papers.key_findings:
Ironic rebound occurs in LLMs after negation instructions, with semantic distractors triggering the strongest rebound.
Repetition distractors support suppression, while semantic and syntactic distractors lead to rebound.
Models with sharper polarity separation (between neutral and negative framings) show longer-lasting rebound (higher L50).
Circuit analysis reveals early layers suppress forbidden tokens, while a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplify them, causing rebound.
Rebound effect varies across models; GPT-OSS-20B is an outlier showing minimal rebound.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic, templated prompts rather than naturalistic conversational contexts.
Reliance on log-probabilities rather than actual text generation.
Focus on English and single-token target concepts.
Only three distractor types (semantic, syntactic, repetition).
Artificial 'do not mention X' instructions differ from real-world content policies.
future_direction: Mechanistic interpretability work to identify specific circuits responsible for ironic rebound.
Explore more naturalistic settings, including conversational contexts.
Investigate the anomalous behavior of GPT-OSS-20B and mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Negation instructions such as 'do not mention $X$' can paradoxically increase the accessibility of $X$ in human thought, a phenomenon known as ironic rebound. Large language models (LLMs) face the same challenge: suppressing a concept requires internally activating it, which may prime rebound instead of avoidance. We investigated this tension with two experiments. \textbf{(1) Load \& content}: after a negation instruction, we vary distractor text (semantic, syntactic, repetition) and measure rebound strength. \textbf{(2) Polarity separation}: We test whether models distinguish neutral from negative framings of the same concept and whether this separation predicts rebound persistence. Results show that rebound consistently arises immediately after negation and intensifies with longer or semantic distractors, while repetition supports suppression. Stronger polarity separation correlates with more persistent rebound. Together, these findings, complemented by a circuit tracing analysis that identifies sparse middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress, link cognitive predictions of ironic rebound with mechanistic insights into long-context interference. To support future work, we release ReboundBench, a dataset of $5,000$ systematically varied negation prompts designed to probe rebound in LLMs.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we control the knowledge selection behavior of large language models (LLMs) when there is a conflict between their parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in the hidden states of LLMs, enabling precise control over knowledge selection behavior during inference to resolve context-memory conflicts.
papers.conclusion: SPARE provides an effective and efficient training-free method for controlling knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, offering a promising approach to managing knowledge conflicts without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected by probing the residual stream of LLMs, with the strongest signal appearing in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively steers LLMs to use either contextual or parametric knowledge, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
The residual stream exhibits a significantly more skewed representation when the model uses contextual knowledge compared to when it uses parametric knowledge.
SPARE requires editing only a very small set of SAE features (e.g., less than 0.05% for Gemma2-9B) to achieve control.
The method is more effective at changing the model's behavior from using contextual to parametric knowledge than other inference-time methods.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on pre-trained SAEs, so it may not apply to models where such SAEs are unavailable or cannot be efficiently trained.
The experiments are conducted on specific open-domain QA tasks; generalization to other task types (e.g., complex reasoning, long-form generation) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in a binary fashion (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), whereas real-world decisions may require more nuanced approaches.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context -- this phenomenon, known as \emph{context-memory knowledge conflicts}, can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. Analysing the internal activations of LLMs, we find that they can internally register the signals of knowledge conflict at mid-layers. Such signals allow us to detect whether a knowledge conflict occurs and use \emph{inference-time} intervention strategies to resolve it. In this work, we propose \textsc{SpARE}, a \emph{training-free} representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) to control the knowledge selection behaviour of LLMs. \textsc{SpARE} identifies the functional features that control the knowledge selection behaviours and applies them to edit the internal activations of LLMs at inference time. Our experimental results show that \textsc{SpARE} can effectively control the usage of either knowledge source to resolve knowledge conflict in open-domain question-answering tasks, surpassing existing representation engineering methods ($+10\%$) as well as contrastive decoding methods ($+15\%$).

papers.title: SafeSwitch: Steering Unsafe LLM Behavior via Internal Activation Signals
papers.research_question: How can internal activation signals in LLMs be used to predict and dynamically regulate unsafe behavior, balancing safety and utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeSwitch, a framework that uses a safety prober to monitor internal states and dynamically activate a refusal head to mitigate unsafe outputs, reducing harmful responses by ~80% while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeSwitch demonstrates LLMs' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced, dynamic, and effective safety controls.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs inherently encode safety-related information (recognition of unsafe instructions and intent to respond) within their internal states.
A two-stage safety prober can predict unsafe behavior with high accuracy (F1 >90%) by decomposing the task into instruction safety and model compliance.
SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries (SORRY-Bench, TrustLLM) while maintaining strong utility on benign benchmarks.
SafeSwitch achieves a Pareto optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baselines like always-on refusal heads or safety prompts.
The method is parameter-efficient, tuning less than 6% of the original model parameters (prober and refusal head).
papers.limitation: The safety prober can produce false positives (over-refusal) and false negatives (missing unsafe responses), with performance varying across query types and benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional capabilities across various tasks but also pose risks by generating harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms, while improving model safety, often lead to overly cautious behavior and fail to fully leverage LLMs' internal cognitive processes. Inspired by humans' reflective thinking capability, we first show that LLMs can similarly perform internal assessments about safety in their internal states. Building on this insight, we propose SafeSwitch, a dynamic framework that regulates unsafe outputs by utilizing the prober-based internal state monitor that actively detects harmful intentions, and activates a safety head that leads to safer and more conservative responses only when necessary. SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries while maintaining strong utility, reaching a Pareto optimal among several methods. Our method is also advantageous over traditional methods in offering more informative, context-aware refusals, and achieves these benefits while only tuning less than 6% of the original parameters. SafeSwitch demonstrates large language models' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced and effective safety controls. Codes for this work are available at https://github.com/Hanpx20/SafeSwitch.

papers.title: Don't Make It Up: Preserving Ignorance Awareness in LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we fine-tune LLMs to incorporate new knowledge without eroding their aligned epistemic abstention behavior (the ability to acknowledge when the model does not know)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SEAT, a fine-tuning method that combines sparse updates and entity-perturbed regularization to preserve a model's epistemic abstention (ability to say 'I don't know') while adapting it to new knowledge, without requiring alignment data or post-hoc re-alignment.
papers.conclusion: SEAT is an effective method for preserving epistemic abstention during knowledge adaptation, establishing preservation of abstention as a useful objective for safer model adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
SEAT preserves epistemic abstention on unseen queries (improving human-evaluated abstention by 18%–101% over baselines) while maintaining near-perfect target knowledge acquisition.
Both sparse training and entity-perturbed regularization are essential for SEAT's strong performance; ablations show each component alone is insufficient.
SEAT constrains activation drift on unseen data, keeping representations anchored near the base model's, while allowing meaningful shifts for fine-tuning data.
SEAT outperforms a range of baselines including full fine-tuning, LoRA, EWC, CLoRA, R-tuning, and experience replay in preserving abstention behavior.
SEAT preserves downstream utility across a diverse range of tasks (e.g., truthfulness, QA, reasoning) compared to the base model.
papers.limitation:
The optimal sparsity ratio needs to be tuned to balance learning efficacy and abstention preservation.
The method is empirically grounded and does not provide formal guarantees.
papers.abstract: Existing work on mitigating catastrophic forgetting during large language models (LLMs) fine-tuning for new knowledge instances has primarily focused on preserving performance on previously seen data, while critically overlooking the collapse of essential capabilities instilled through alignment, most notably the model's ability to faithfully express epistemic uncertainty (a property we term 'Ignorance Awareness'). In this work, we formalize the notion of Ignorance Awareness and illustrate that conventional fine-tuning methods can result in substantial activation displacement. This displacement undermines the critical capability of ignorance awareness, leading to undesirable behaviors such as hallucinations. To address this challenge, we introduce SEAT, a simple and principled fine-tuning approach that not only enables the model to effectively acquire new knowledge instances but also preserves its aligned ignorance awareness. SEAT integrates two key components: (1) sparse tuning that constrains activation drift, and (2) a novel entity perturbation method designed to counter knowledge entanglement. Experimental results demonstrate that, across both real-world and synthetic datasets, SEAT significantly outperforms baselines in preserving ignorance awareness while retaining optimal fine-tuning performance, offering a more robust solution for LLM fine-tuning.

papers.title: Robust LLM safeguarding via refusal feature adversarial training
papers.research_question: How do adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs, and can we design an efficient adversarial training method based on the mechanism of refusal feature ablation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that simulates attacks via refusal feature ablation to improve robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers that adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating refusal features, and proposes ReFAT, an efficient adversarial training method that improves robustness while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial attacks jailbreak LLMs by ablating a refusal feature in the residual stream, as shown by high cosine similarity between attack-induced shifts and the refusal feature direction.
Refusal feature ablation approximates the worst-case adversarial perturbation that minimizes model safety score.
ReFAT, which ablates refusal features during training, improves LLM robustness against a wide range of adversarial attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, HumanJailbreaks).
ReFAT achieves comparable or better robustness than existing adversarial training methods with significantly lower computational cost.
ReFAT preserves general model utility, as measured by MMLU and MT-Bench, and does not cause excessive over-refusals.
papers.limitation: ReFAT may not defend against attacks that use linguistic contexts very different from the harmless instructions used to compute refusal features, such as multilingual attacks or under-represented English vernacular.
future_direction: Use a more diverse set of instructions to compute refusal features to improve robustness against multilingual and varied linguistic attacks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can elicit harmful responses. Defending against such attacks remains challenging due to the opacity of jailbreaking mechanisms and the high computational cost of training LLMs robustly. We demonstrate that adversarial attacks share a universal mechanism for circumventing LLM safeguards that works by ablating a dimension in the residual stream embedding space called the refusal feature. We further show that the operation of refusal feature ablation (RFA) approximates the worst-case perturbation of offsetting model safety. Based on these findings, we propose Refusal Feature Adversarial Training (ReFAT), a novel algorithm that efficiently performs LLM adversarial training by simulating the effect of input-level attacks via RFA. Experiment results show that ReFAT significantly improves the robustness of three popular LLMs against a wide range of adversarial attacks, with considerably less computational overhead compared to existing adversarial training methods.

papers.title: How Training Data Shapes the Use of Parametric and In-Context Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What training data properties enable language models to robustly utilize both parametric and in-context knowledge and resolve conflicts between them?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three training data properties—intra-document repetition, within-document inconsistency, and skewed knowledge frequency distribution—that must co-occur for robust knowledge utilization and conflict resolution in language models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides the first systematic analysis showing that intra-document repetition, inconsistency, and skewed knowledge distribution are essential for robust knowledge utilization, offering practical guidance for training data design.
papers.key_findings:
Intra-document repetition enables the co-emergence of parametric and in-context knowledge utilization, with in-context knowledge utilization emerging first.
A moderate level of within-document inconsistency prevents over-reliance on in-context knowledge and induces a preference transition towards parametric knowledge as training progresses.
A skewed knowledge frequency distribution preserves in-context knowledge utilization capabilities by ensuring continuous usage for rare entities.
These properties jointly enable balanced reliance on both knowledge sources and confidence-dependent arbitration.
Instruction tuning can reshape knowledge arbitration strategies, increasing reliance on in-context knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic biography datasets which may not fully reflect natural language richness.
Focuses on knowledge conflicts based on internal confidence, leaving other retrieval-augmented generation scenarios for future work.
future_direction: Investigation of diverse retrieval-augmented generation scenarios such as retrieval errors, partial relevance, and multi-document conflicts.
papers.abstract: Large language models leverage not only parametric knowledge acquired during training but also in-context knowledge provided at inference time, despite the absence of explicit training objectives for using both sources. Prior work has further shown that when these knowledge sources conflict, models resolve the tension based on their internal confidence, preferring parametric knowledge for high-confidence facts while deferring to contextual information for less familiar ones. However, the training conditions that give rise to such knowledge utilization behaviors remain unclear. To address this gap, we conduct controlled experiments in which we train language models while systematically manipulating key properties of the training data. Our results reveal a counterintuitive finding: three properties commonly regarded as detrimental must co-occur for robust knowledge utilization and conflict resolution to emerge: (i) intra-document repetition of information, (ii) a moderate degree of within-document inconsistency, and (iii) a skewed knowledge frequency distribution. We further validate that the same training dynamics observed in our controlled setting also arise during real-world language model pretraining, and we analyze how post-training procedures can reshape models' knowledge preferences. Together, our findings provide concrete empirical guidance for training language models that harmoniously integrate parametric and in-context knowledge.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unlearning: Robust Knowledge Unlearning and Editing via Mechanistic Localization
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability improve the precision and effectiveness of knowledge editing and unlearning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic unlearning, which localizes edits to fact lookup mechanisms, improves robustness in knowledge editing and unlearning across different prompts and resists relearning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic unlearning via FLU localization provides a robust framework for knowledge editing and unlearning, outperforming output-tracing methods.
papers.key_findings:
FLU localization leads to more robust edits/unlearning across different input/output formats compared to output-tracing methods.
FLU localization resists attempts to relearn the unwanted information, making unlearning more persistent.
FLU localization reduces unintended side effects on general language modeling capabilities compared to baselines.
FLU localization modifies internal latent knowledge to reflect edited answers more effectively than other methods.
Output-tracing methods target extraction mechanisms rather than fact lookup, leading to less robust edits.
papers.abstract: Methods for knowledge editing and unlearning in large language models seek to edit or remove undesirable knowledge or capabilities without compromising general language modeling performance. This work investigates how mechanistic interpretability -- which, in part, aims to identify model components (circuits) associated to specific interpretable mechanisms that make up a model capability -- can improve the precision and effectiveness of editing and unlearning. We find a stark difference in unlearning and edit robustness when training components localized by different methods. We highlight an important distinction between methods that localize components based primarily on preserving outputs, and those finding high level mechanisms with predictable intermediate states. In particular, localizing edits/unlearning to components associated with the lookup-table mechanism for factual recall 1) leads to more robust edits/unlearning across different input/output formats, and 2) resists attempts to relearn the unwanted information, while also reducing unintended side effects compared to baselines, on both a sports facts dataset and the CounterFact dataset across multiple models. We also find that certain localized edits disrupt the latent knowledge in the model more than any other baselines, making unlearning more robust to various attacks.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: How Does Metacognition Contribute to the Regulation of Learning? An Integrative Approach
papers.abstract: The paper addresses issues related to the accuracy of metacognitive monitoring and the effectiveness of control.Based on the enriched model of metacognition (Efklides, 2008), the facets and levels of functioning of metacognition are presented as well as the processes underlying each facet at the various levels of metacognition.Review of current research on monitoring (i.e., metacognitive experiences and metacognitive knowledge) suggests that monitoring can be inaccurate but factors such as prior knowledge, feedback, and attending to task context and response features can increase accuracy.Control, on the other hand, can be triggered by cognition, affect and metacognition.Research evidence on the relations between monitoring and control suggests that monitoring accuracy can support more effective control decisions but not always.Moreover, control can be ineffective due to lack of resources.What is of interest is that control decisions are often influenced by motivational considerations rather than objective task difficulty and through effects of affect on metacognitive monitoring.This implies that metacognition should be viewed within a broader theoretical framework of self-regulation such as the Metacognitive and Affective model of Self-regulated Learning (Efklides, 2011).The implications of the model are discussed as well as the challenges for future research on metacognition.

papers.title: Metacognition and polyregulation in daily self‐control conflicts
papers.abstract: Metacognition is important for self-regulated learning, and it has recently been argued that it may play an important role in self-control more generally. We studied multiple aspects of metacognition in self-control, namely metacognitive knowledge including a person's repertoire ("toolbox") of different self-regulatory strategies, metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, and evaluation), and polyregulation (using more self-regulatory strategies in a single self-control conflict) as predictors of people's self-control success in daily life. In a preregistered experience sampling study, N = 503 participants reported their self-control conflicts up to eight times per day for 10 days, yielding 9,639 reports of daily self-control conflicts. Analyses showed that higher levels of metacognitive knowledge, planning, monitoring, evaluation, and polyregulation as well as a larger strategy repertoire were associated with higher levels of success in resolving daily self-control conflicts. Additionally, higher levels of trait self-control were associated with higher levels of metacognitive knowledge, planning, and monitoring. These findings highlight the importance of metacognition and polyregulation for successful self-control.

papers.title: Confounding in Studies on Metacognition: A Preliminary Causal Analysis Framework
papers.abstract: By definition, metacognitive processes may monitor or regulate various stages of first-order processing. By combining causal analysis with hypotheses expressed by other authors we derive the theoretical and methodological consequences of this special relation between metacognition and the underlying processes. In particular, we prove that because multiple processing stages may be monitored or regulated and because metacognition may form latent feedback loops, (1) without strong additional causal assumptions, typical measures of metacognitive monitoring or regulation are confounded; (2) without strong additional causal assumptions, typical methods of controlling for first-order task performance (i.e., calibration, staircase, including first-order task performance in a regression analysis, or analyzing correct and incorrect trials separately) not only do not deconfound measures of metacognition but may even introduce bias; (3) that the first two problems cannot be solved by using simple models of decision-making derived from Signal Detection Theory. We conclude the paper by advocating robust methods of discovering properties of latent mechanisms.

papers.title: Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers
papers.abstract: Abstract When responding to knowledge questions, people monitor their confidence in the knowledge they retrieve from memory and strategically regulate their responses so as to provide answers that are both correct and informative. The current study investigated the association between subjective confidence and the use of two response strategies: seeking help and withholding answers by responding “I don’t know”. Seeking help has been extensively studied as a resource management strategy in self-regulated learning, but has been largely neglected in metacognition research. In contrast, withholding answers has received less attention in educational studies than in metacognition research. Across three experiments, we compared the relationship between subjective confidence and strategy use in conditions where participants could choose between submitting answers and seeking help, between submitting and withholding answers, or between submitting answers, seeking help, and withholding answers. Results consistently showed that the association between confidence and help seeking was weaker than that between confidence and withholding answers. This difference was found for participants from two different populations, remained when participants received monetary incentives for accurate answers, and replicated across two forms of help. Our findings suggest that seeking help is guided by a wider variety of considerations than withholding answers, with some considerations going beyond improving the immediate accuracy of one’s answers. We discuss implications for research on metacognition and regarding question answering in educational and other contexts.

papers.title: Heuristic Cues for Meta-Reasoning Judgments
papers.abstract: Metacognitive research aims to explain how people regulate their effort when performing cognitive tasks, to expose conditions that support reliable monitoring of chance for success, and to provide a basis for developing improvement guidelines. The essence of the domain is that monitoring drives control: people continually self-assess their chance for success before, during, and after performing a cognitive task, and use these judgments to guide their effort-allocation decisions (e.g., whether to reconsider an answer option, change strategy, seek help, or give up). Thus, factors that underlie metacognitive judgments affect the efficiency with which people perform cognitive tasks. This paper focuses on meta-reasoning – the monitoring and control processes that apply to reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making tasks. So far, relatively little is known about heuristic cues used for inferring meta-reasoning judgments. This paper reviews the known heuristic cues and offers methodological guidelines for a critical reading of existing research and for designing high-quality studies that will advance this important domain.

papers.title: Metacognition in decision making
papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly and accurately judge their subjective probability of being correct in a given decision, leading to the view that metacognition is integral to decision making. This thesis reports a series of experiments assessing people’s confidence and error-detection judgements. These different types of metacognitive judgements are highly similar with regard to their methodology, but have been studied largely separately. I provide data indicating that these judgements are fundamentally linked and that they rely on shared cognitive and neural mechanisms. As a first step towards such a joint account of confidence and error detection, I present simulations from a computational model that is based on the notion these judgements are based on the same underlying processes. I next focus on how metacognitive signals are utilised to enhance cognitive control by means of a modulation of information seeking. I report data from a study in which participants received performance feedback, testing the hypothesis that participants will focus more on feedback when they are uncertain whether they were correct in the current trial, whilst ignoring feedback when they are certain regarding their accuracy. A final question addressed in this thesis asks which information contributes internally to the formation of metacognitive judgements, given that it remains a challenge for most models of confidence to explain the precise mechanisms by which confidence reflects accuracy, under which circumstances this correlation is reduced, and the role other influences might have, such as the inherent reliability of a source of evidence. The results reported here suggest that multiple variables – such as response time and reliability of evidence – play a role in the generation of metacognitive judgements. Inter-individual differences with regard to the utilisation of these cues to confidence are tested. Taken together, my results suggest that metacognition is crucially involved in decision making and cognitive control.

papers.title: Control in Response Inhibition
papers.abstract: This chapter reviews recent behavioural and computational work on response inhibition. In the response-inhibition literature, individual or group differences are often attributed to variation in the effectiveness of a single inhibitory control function. It discusses mainly ‘reactive’, ‘proactive’, and ‘associatively mediated’ forms of inhibitory control. The chapter focuses on the stop-signal paradigm because it allows researchers to estimate the covert latency of response inhibition: the stop-signal reaction time (SSRT). In response-inhibition tasks, people often adjust their behaviour in anticipation of future acts of inhibitory control. Proactive adjustments are made at the beginning of a block or on a trial-by-trial basis, suggesting a flexible cognitive system that adjusts itself quickly in response to novel contextual information. Suppression of prestimulus motor activity is observed in go/no-go and choice RT paradigms, which points to a general proactive control mechanism that prevents premature responding.

papers.title: Optimal Metacognitive Control of Memory Recall
papers.abstract: Most of us have experienced moments when we could not recall some piece of information, but felt that it was just out of reach. Research in metamemory has established that such judgments are often accurate; but what adaptive purpose do they serve? Here, we present an optimal model of how metacognitive monitoring (feeling of knowing) could dynamically inform metacognitive control of memory (the direction of retrieval efforts). In two experiments, we find that, consistent with the optimal model, people report having a stronger memory for targets they are likely to recall, and direct their search efforts accordingly, cutting off search when it is unlikely to succeed and prioritizing search for stronger memories. Our results suggest that metamemory is indeed adaptive, and motivate the development of process-level theories that account for the dynamic interplay between monitoring and control.

papers.title: The effects of distraction on metacognition and metacognition on distraction: evidence from recognition memory
papers.abstract: The effects of auditory distraction in memory tasks have, to date, been examined with procedures that minimize participants' control over their own memory processes. Surprisingly little attention has been paid to metacognitive control factors which might affect memory performance. In this study, we investigate the effects of auditory distraction on metacognitive control of memory, examining the effects of auditory distraction in recognition tasks utilizing the metacognitive framework of Koriat and Goldsmith (1996), to determine whether strategic regulation of memory accuracy is impacted by auditory distraction. Results replicated previous findings in showing that auditory distraction impairs memory performance in tasks minimizing participants' metacognitive control (forced-report test). However, the results revealed also that when metacognitive control is allowed (free-report tests), auditory distraction impacts upon a range of metacognitive indices. In the present study, auditory distraction undermined accuracy of metacognitive monitoring (resolution), reduced confidence in responses provided and, correspondingly, increased participants' propensity to withhold responses in free-report recognition. Crucially, changes in metacognitive processes were related to impairment in free-report recognition performance, as the use of the "don't know" option under distraction led to a reduction in the number of correct responses volunteered in free-report tests. Overall, the present results show how auditory distraction exerts its influence on memory performance via both memory and metamemory processes.

papers.title: Metacognition and Self-Control: An Integrative Framework
papers.abstract: Self-control describes the processes by which individuals control their habits, desires, and impulses in the service of long-term goals. Research has identified important components of self-control and proposed theoretical frameworks integrating these components (e.g., Inzlicht et al., 2021; Kotabe &amp; Hofmann, 2015). In our perspective, these frameworks, however, do not yet fully incorporate important metacognitive aspects of self-control. We therefore introduce a framework explicating the role of metacognition for self-control. This framework extends existing frameworks, primarily from the domains of self-regulated learning and problem-solving (e.g., Schraw &amp; Moshman, 1995; Zimmermann, 2000), and integrates past and contemporary research and theorizing on self-control that involves aspects of metacognition. It considers two groups of metacognitive components, namely (1) individual metacognitive characteristics, that is a person´s declarative, procedural, and conditional metacognitive knowledge about self-control, as well as their self-awareness (or metacognitive awareness), and (2) metacognitive regulatory processes that unfold before a self-control conflict (forethought, and prevention), when a self-control conflict is identified, during a self-control conflict (regulation and monitoring), and after a self-control conflict (reflection and evaluation). The proposed framework integrates existing research and will be useful for highlighting new directions for research on the role of metacognition for self-control success and failure.

papers.title: Individual Differences in Uncertainty Responsiveness and Stroop Interference
papers.abstract: The study of metacognition is rooted in the observation of behaviors under states of uncertainty (e.g., Smith et al., 1995). Individuals who are more responsive to uncertainty tend to show greater interference effects in a Stroop color-word naming task compared to those who are less responsive to uncertainty (Washburn, Smith, & Taglialatela, 2005). Individual differences in Stroop interference also have been shown to reflect relative differences in response competition (Washburn, 1994) and rule-maintenance ability (Kane & Engle, 2003). Why would individuals who respond to uncertainty most adaptively be characterized by the worst attention-control skills? The current study was designed to measure the individual contribution of sensitivity to response competition and rule maintenance ability to the pre-established relationship between Stroop interference and uncertainty responsiveness. Though participants performed as expected in both tasks, the previously reported relationship between Stroop interference and uncertainty responsiveness was not observed.

papers.title: Optimal Hedging Levels and Hedging Effectiveness in Cattle Feeding
papers.abstract: Optimal hedging level, minimum-risk hedging level, and hedging effectiveness are defined in a manner consistent with portfolio theory and used to analyze hedging potential in cattle feeding. Estimated upper limits on optimal hedging levels ranged from 0.56 to 0.88 unit of short futures per unit of four types of slaughter cattle produced at five locations. When futures trading costs are taken into account, optimal hedging levels are depressed below these limits, depending upon the resource availabilities and profit expectations of individual firms. Location, grade, and sex of the cattle fed have small effects on optimal hedging levels and hedging effectiveness.

papers.title: A Multiverse Analysis of Early Attempts to Replicate Memory Suppression with the Think/No-think Task
papers.abstract: In 2001, Anderson and Green (2001) showed memory suppression using a novel Think/No-think (TNT) task. When participants attempted to prevent studied words from entering awareness, they reported fewer of those words than baseline words in subsequent cued recall (i.e., suppression effect).
