This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Sparse Neurons Carry Strong Signals of Question Ambiguity in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is question ambiguity encoded in the internal representations of LLMs, and can it be detected and controlled at the neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Question ambiguity is sparsely encoded in a small set of neurons (AENs) in LLMs, and steering these neurons can control the model's behavior from answering to abstention.
papers.conclusion: Ambiguity is encoded in a compact, model-specific subspace of neurons, enabling interpretable and controllable behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ambiguity is linearly encoded in LLM internal representations and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probes.
A small set of neurons (AENs) encode ambiguity, with as few as one neuron being sufficient.
Probes trained only on AENs achieve strong performance and generalize across datasets.
Activation steering on AENs causally shifts model behavior from direct answering to abstention.
AENs emerge in shallow layers and capture a large proportion of the full steering effect.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to three instruction-tuned LLMs and two datasets, and broader validation is needed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to the token level to see how ambiguity arises within a question and influences model uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Ambiguity is pervasive in real-world questions, yet large language models (LLMs) often respond with confident answers rather than seeking clarification. In this work, we show that question ambiguity is linearly encoded in the internal representations of LLMs and can be both detected and controlled at the neuron level. During the model's pre-filling stage, we identify that a small number of neurons, as few as one, encode question ambiguity information. Probes trained on these Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons (AENs) achieve strong performance on ambiguity detection and generalize across datasets, outperforming prompting-based and representation-based baselines. Layerwise analysis reveals that AENs emerge from shallow layers, suggesting early encoding of ambiguity signals in the model's processing pipeline. Finally, we show that through manipulating AENs, we can control LLM's behavior from direct answering to abstention. Our findings reveal that LLMs form compact internal representations of question ambiguity, enabling interpretable and controllable behavior.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Disentangling Deception and Hallucination Failures in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs by separating knowledge existence from behavior expression?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs, and constructs a controlled environment for analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Representational separability analysis shows that knowledge existence is a dominant signal in distinguishing failure modes.
Sparse autoencoder reveals feature groupings associated with different behavioral cases, indicating a global split driven by knowledge existence.
Activation steering can induce bidirectional transitions between correct and deceptive behaviors, demonstrating causal control over behavior expression.
Hallucination cases are not reversible via activation steering, highlighting the distinction between knowledge absence and suppression.
Deception involves suppression of knowledge expression rather than knowledge removal, as verified through jailbreak probing.
papers.abstract: Failures in large language models (LLMs) are often analyzed from a behavioral perspective, where incorrect outputs in factual question answering are commonly associated with missing knowledge. In this work, focusing on entity-based factual queries, we suggest that such a view may conflate different failure mechanisms, and propose an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression. Under this formulation, hallucination and deception correspond to two qualitatively different failure modes that may appear similar at the output level but differ in their underlying mechanisms. To study this distinction, we construct a controlled environment for entity-centric factual questions in which knowledge is preserved while behavioral expression is selectively altered, enabling systematic analysis of four behavioral cases. We analyze these failure modes through representation separability, sparse interpretability, and inference-time activation steering.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
papers.research_question: How do large language models acquire, retain, and forget concepts during continual pretraining? Specifically, how do internal concept representations correlate with concept acquisition and forgetting, and how do they relate to interference and synergy among multiple concepts and knowledge types during joint training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a circuit-level analysis of concept learning in LLMs during continual pre-training, revealing that concept circuits provide signals for learning and forgetting dynamics, and show patterns like stage-wise temporal changes and interference/synergy effects.
papers.conclusion: The work offers a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and informs the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting.
Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization.
Concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training.
Semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones.
Conceptual knowledge differs in transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others.
papers.limitation:
Limited model scale, focusing only on GPT-2 Large and LLaMA-3.2-1B, not larger models.
Exploration of actionable training strategies is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending analysis to larger-scale models.
Exploring circuit-aware training effort allocation and interference-aware data scheduling.
papers.abstract: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal Concept Circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate Graph Metrics to characterize circuit structure. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization; (3) concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training; (4) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (5) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings offer a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and inform the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Steering to Say No: Configurable Refusal via Activation Steering in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust and efficient configurable refusal approach for VLMs that can adapt to diverse user needs?
papers.core_contribution: CR-VLM is a robust and efficient framework for configurable refusal in VLMs using activation steering, enabling user-adaptive safety alignment without modifying the backbone model.
papers.conclusion: CR-VLM provides an effective, efficient, and robust approach for configurable refusal in VLMs, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
CR-VLM achieves high refusal rates on out-of-scope queries and low over-refusal on in-scope queries, outperforming baseline methods.
Teacher-forced activation extraction yields stronger refusal signals compared to prompt-based extraction.
The orthogonality loss term effectively mitigates over-refusal by decoupling intervention directions for in-scope and out-of-scope samples.
The vision loss encourages the model to attend to visual cues, improving refusal behavior grounded in visual evidence.
Activation distribution analysis shows that CR-VLM shifts out-of-scope representations toward refusal while preserving in-scope representations.
papers.limitation:
Relies on open-source models with accessible hidden states, restricting applicability to closed-source models.
Current experiments focus on one constraint at a time; multi-constraint settings are left for future work.
Lack of standardized benchmarks for explicit policy-conditioned scenarios limits evaluation in such settings.
future_direction: Extend CR-VLM to closed-source models where internal activations are not exposed.
Systematically study multi-constraint settings through composition.
Explore policy-conditioned configurable refusal once suitable benchmarks become available.
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Vision Language Models (VLMs), refusal mechanisms have become a critical component for ensuring responsible and safe model behavior. However, existing refusal strategies are largely \textit{one-size-fits-all} and fail to adapt to diverse user needs and contextual constraints, leading to either under-refusal or over-refusal. In this work, we firstly explore the challenges mentioned above and develop \textbf{C}onfigurable \textbf{R}efusal in \textbf{VLM}s (\textbf{CR-VLM}), a robust and efficient approach for {\em configurable} refusal based on activation steering. CR-VLM consists of three integrated components: (1) extracting a configurable refusal vector via a teacher-forced mechanism to amplify the refusal signal; (2) introducing a gating mechanism that mitigates over-refusal by preserving acceptance for in-scope queries; and (3) designing a counterfactual vision enhancement module that aligns visual representations with refusal requirements. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets and various VLMs demonstrate that CR-VLM achieves effective, efficient, and robust configurable refusals, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment in VLMs.

papers.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
papers.research_question: How do long-context language models retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the input?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and characterizes 'retrieval heads', a sparse set of attention heads responsible for retrieving information from long contexts, and shows they are universal, intrinsic, and causally important for factuality and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval heads implement a conditional copy algorithm and are the primary reason why long-context models can pass the Needle-in-a-Haystack test; their activation explains model factuality versus hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are universal and sparse, existing in all tested long-context models and constituting less than 5% of attention heads.
Retrieval heads are intrinsic, already present in base models and reused in derived models (e.g., via continued pretraining or fine-tuning).
Retrieval heads are dynamically activated based on the specific tokens and context required for retrieval.
Retrieval heads are causal; pruning them leads to retrieval failure and hallucination, while pruning non-retrieval heads does not.
Retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, which require frequent reference to input information, but have less impact on tasks relying on internal knowledge.
future_direction: Fostering future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
Discovering more algorithm and functionalities implemented by other types of attention heads.
Applying insights to KV cache compression by pruning non-retrieval head caches.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent progress in long-context language models, it remains elusive how transformer-based models exhibit the capability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context. This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify intriguing properties of retrieval heads:(1) universal: all the explored models with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small portion (less than 5\%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending the context length by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random non-retrieval heads does not affect the model's retrieval ability. We further show that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context. Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the input tokens. We believe our insights will foster future research on reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

papers.title: Surgical Knowledge Rewrite in Compact LLMs: An 'Unlearn-then-Learn' Strategy with ($IA^3$) for Localized Factual Modulation and Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
papers.research_question: How to achieve precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs for conflicting factual updates while mitigating catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mechanistically informed 'unlearn-then-learn' strategy with IA3 that achieves precise knowledge editing in compact LLMs, with high accuracy for new facts and minimal catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The method enables deterministic, precise, and localized knowledge editing, advancing LLM knowledge management with enhanced safety and control.
papers.key_findings:
Achieves 98.50% accuracy for the new fact and 96.00% forget rate for the original fact.
Shows 72.00% F_control accuracy, significantly mitigating catastrophic forgetting compared to direct fine-tuning.
Demonstrates 'soft forgetting' where original knowledge is suppressed but remains latently accessible.
Outperforms direct fine-tuning methods like LoRA and IA3 in localization and fact modulation.
Uses circuit localization to inform targeted PEFT application for effective editing.
papers.limitation: The method may struggle to scale with sequential unlearning requests or larger forget sets in very large LLMs.
future_direction: Scalability of the strategy to larger LLMs
Further mechanistic insights into 'soft forgetting' and auditing unlearning
Potential for multi-fact and chained knowledge edits
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with dynamic knowledge updates, especially when new information conflicts with deeply embedded facts. Such conflicting factual edits often lead to two critical issues: resistance to adopting the new fact and severe catastrophic forgetting of unrelated knowledge. This paper introduces and evaluates a novel "unlearn-then-learn" strategy for precise knowledge editing in LLMs, leveraging the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique, Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations ($IA^3$). Crucially, this two-stage approach is powered by an initial circuit localization phase that identifies and targets the specific internal components responsible for encoding the conflicting fact. Through a rigorous experimental methodology on microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, we demonstrate that this mechanistically informed two-stage approach achieves near-perfect accuracy (98.50%) for the new, modulated fact while simultaneously effectively suppressing the original conflicting fact (96.00% forget rate). Critically, our strategy exhibits unprecedented localization (72.00% F_control accuracy), dramatically mitigating catastrophic forgetting observed in direct fine-tuning approaches (which showed as low as ~20% F_control accuracy), a direct benefit of our targeted interpretability-guided intervention. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals a nuanced mechanism of "soft forgetting," where original knowledge is suppressed from default retrieval but remains latent and conditionally accessible, enhancing model safety and control. These findings represent a significant advancement towards precise, localized, and safe knowledge management in compact LLMs.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution
papers.research_question: Does the suppression of parametric knowledge in the residual stream arise from the radial dilution of the signal's magnitude, or from an angular displacement induced by orthogonal interference?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs resolve in-context knowledge conflicts through orthogonal interference in the residual stream, rotating hidden states rather than diluting signal magnitude, challenging scalar confidence metrics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs resolve knowledge conflicts via orthogonal interference in the residual stream, simulating adoption without erasing internal knowledge, highlighting the need for vectorial monitoring over scalar metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: Llama See, Llama Do: A Mechanistic Perspective on Contextual Entrainment and Distraction in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do language models become distracted by irrelevant contextual information, and what is the mechanistic basis for this distraction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies contextual entrainment, a novel phenomenon where LMs assign higher probabilities to tokens that appear in the context, and discovers entrainment heads that control this effect, providing a mechanistic perspective on distraction.
papers.conclusion: Contextual entrainment is a novel mechanistic phenomenon that plays a crucial role in LM distraction, and interpretability techniques can provide insights for real-world applications such as RAG.
papers.key_findings:
LMs assign significantly higher logits/probabilities to tokens that have appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens (contextual entrainment).
The magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors, with counterfactual prompts having a stronger effect than factual ones.
A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) are responsible for contextual entrainment; disabling them attenuates the effect.
Entrainment heads are relation-specific, not model-specific.
Removing entrainment heads has minimal impact on other LM capabilities like factual recall and in-context learning.
papers.limitation:
Did not conduct experiments using larger LMs due to resource limitations.
Only used the LRE dataset and not standard RAG datasets.
Do not propose an application to mitigate the distraction problem.
future_direction: Reproduce results using larger models.
Validate findings using standard RAG datasets.
Further steps toward addressing the distraction problem.
papers.abstract: We observe a novel phenomenon, contextual entrainment, across a wide range of language models (LMs) and prompt settings, providing a new mechanistic perspective on how LMs become distracted by ``irrelevant'' contextual information in the input prompt. Specifically, LMs assign significantly higher logits (or probabilities) to any tokens that have previously appeared in the context prompt, even for random tokens. This suggests that contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, occurring independently of the relevance or semantic relation of the tokens to the question or the rest of the sentence. We find statistically significant evidence that the magnitude of contextual entrainment is influenced by semantic factors. Counterfactual prompts have a greater effect compared to factual ones, suggesting that while contextual entrainment is a mechanistic phenomenon, it is modulated by semantic factors. We hypothesise that there is a circuit of attention heads -- the entrainment heads -- that corresponds to the contextual entrainment phenomenon. Using a novel entrainment head discovery method based on differentiable masking, we identify these heads across various settings. When we ``turn off'' these heads, i.e., set their outputs to zero, the effect of contextual entrainment is significantly attenuated, causing the model to generate output that capitulates to what it would produce if no distracting context were provided. Our discovery of contextual entrainment, along with our investigation into LM distraction via the entrainment heads, marks a key step towards the mechanistic analysis and mitigation of the distraction problem.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How do different mechanisms interact in the decision-making of LLMs? The paper proposes to trace how one mechanism becomes dominant in the final prediction.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formulates the competition of mechanisms and traces how mechanisms compete within LLMs, identifying critical components and attention positions that control the strength of mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates how to trace the competition of mechanisms in LLMs and reveals insights into how factual and counterfactual mechanisms interact and can be controlled.
papers.key_findings:
In early layers, the factual attribute is encoded in the subject position, while the counterfactual is in the attribute position.
The attention blocks write most of the factual and counterfactual information to the last position.
All the highly activated heads attend to the attribute position regardless of the specific type of information they promote. The factual information flows by penalizing the counterfactual attribute rather than promoting the factual one.
We can up-weight the value of a few very localized values of the attention head matrix to strengthen factual mechanisms substantially.
Similar tokens confuse the model more easily, and larger models suffer more from such confusion.
papers.limitation: Logit inspection can occasionally fail to reflect the actual importance of vocabulary items, especially in the early layers of the network.
future_direction: Extend the competition of mechanisms formulation to more complex mechanisms and multi-step reasoning.
Explore other mechanisms and their competitions in future work.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research aims to bridge the gap between empirical success and our scientific understanding of the inner workings of large language models (LLMs). However, most existing research focuses on analyzing a single mechanism, such as how models copy or recall factual knowledge. In this work, we propose a formulation of competition of mechanisms, which focuses on the interplay of multiple mechanisms instead of individual mechanisms and traces how one of them becomes dominant in the final prediction. We uncover how and where mechanisms compete within LLMs using two interpretability methods: logit inspection and attention modification. Our findings show traces of the mechanisms and their competition across various model components and reveal attention positions that effectively control the strength of certain mechanisms. Code: https://github.com/francescortu/comp-mech. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/francescortu/comp-mech.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Answer When Needed, Forget When Not: Language Models Pretend to Forget via In-Context Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to selectively forget information at test-time based on the query context?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context knowledge unlearning, a method that enables LLMs to selectively forget information at test-time, and reveals that LLMs 'pretend to forget' by making the decision only at the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The method enables LLMs to dynamically forget information at test-time and uncovers that they pretend to forget, advancing towards more ethical and privacy-conscious AI.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves up to 95% forget accuracy while retaining 80% of unrelated knowledge, outperforming baselines.
It works effectively in both in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios.
Internal analysis shows that LLMs generate correct predictions in middle layers but decide to forget only at the last layer, i.e., 'pretend to forget'.
LoRA tuning provides the most balanced performance among tuning methods.
The method maintains general language understanding capabilities with minimal degradation on standard NLP tasks.
papers.limitation:
The method is difficult to apply to closed models accessible only via APIs.
Lack of internal behavior analysis for closed models.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are applied across diverse domains, the ability to selectively unlearn specific information is becoming increasingly essential. For instance, LLMs are expected to selectively provide confidential information to authorized internal users, such as employees or trusted partners, while withholding it from external users, including the general public and unauthorized entities. Therefore, we propose a novel method termed ``in-context knowledge unlearning'', which enables the model to selectively forget information in test-time based on the query context. Our method fine-tunes pre-trained LLMs to enable prompt unlearning of target knowledge within the context, while preserving unrelated information. Experiments on TOFU, AGE and RWKU datasets using Llama2-7B/13B and Mistral-7B models demonstrate that our method achieves up to 95% forget accuracy while retaining 80% of unrelated knowledge, significantly outperforming baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios.
